# A sharp weighted inequality for centroidal planar chords

This is a continuous planar theorem for a balanced collection of individually
centroidal sections. It is an auxiliary result, not a mixed-integer depth
theorem. The heavy-chord reduction was independently found by the parent
and the fiber-functional agent; the parent supplied the subset polynomial
calculation, verified below.

## 1. Statement

Let K be a planar convex body with 0 in its interior. Let p_1,...,p_m be
nonzero vectors such that both p_i and -p_i belong to boundary K. Write
R(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1), and put

    H_i={x:R(p_i) dot x>=0}.

Let theta_i>=0, sum_i theta_i=1, and sum_i theta_i p_i=0. Then

    sum_i theta_i |K intersect H_i| >= (4/9)|K|.           (1)

The constant is sharp: a triangle centered at its centroid, with its three
facet-parallel centroidal chords and the corresponding balanced weights,
has equality.

For these unnormalized cap normals R(p_i), the coarea section factor is
length([-p_i,p_i])/|R(p_i)|=2. Thus the displayed vector balance is exactly
the balance of the continuous point derivatives of these individual cap
areas. The hypothesis that the sections themselves are centered at zero
is essential; merely balancing arbitrary section gradients is weaker.

## 2. Reduction to two or three chords

For fixed p_i the feasible weight set is a compact polytope defined by
nonnegativity, one sum equation and two vector equations. A minimizing
weight vector for the linear left side of (1) has support at most three:
if a support of size at least four were extreme, a nonzero dependence
among its columns (1,p_i) would give a two-sided feasible weight variation.

A one-point support is impossible. If two points support a balance, they
are on opposite rays. Their boundary conditions force p_2=-p_1, and their
weights are both one half. The two closed caps partition K off a line of
area zero, so their weighted area is |K|/2. Collinear three-point cases
reduce to such pairs. It remains to prove (1) for a noncollinear triple
with positive weights.

Each theta_i is at most one half. If theta_i>1/2, balance expresses p_i
as a convex combination of 0 and the two points -p_j, with a positive
coefficient at 0. Since 0 is interior to K, that places p_i in its interior,
a contradiction. First consider the strict case theta_i<1/2.

## 3. Heavy chords reduce the problem to one triangle

The six points ±p_i form a strictly convex centrally symmetric hexagon
H. For example, after an invertible linear map take p_1=(1,0), p_2=(0,1),
p_3=(-a,-b), where a,b>0. The strict weight inequalities say

    a+b>1,       1+b-a>0,       1+a-b>0.

These are precisely the strict hexagon inequalities for the cyclic list
(1,0),(a,b),(0,1),(-1,0),(-a,-b),(0,-1).

The weighted indicator W(x)=sum_i theta_i 1_(H_i)(x) is constant on the
six open angular sectors bounded by the rays ±p_i. Their values alternate
between the three light values theta_i and the three heavy values
1-theta_i. In particular every heavy value is greater than one half.

For each heavy sector cut K by the closed halfplane through that sector's
two marked boundary endpoints which contains zero. The removed part lies
entirely in that heavy sector. Here is a proof retaining arbitrary curved
boundaries. If the endpoint line supports K, nothing is removed. Otherwise
its intersection with K has exactly those endpoints: a boundary point in
the relative interior of a nonsupporting line section would be an interior
point of K. Write the line as a dot x=1. For a removed point x, its radial
projection x/(a dot x) belongs to that line section, since the segment
from 0 to x lies in K. Thus x lies in the cone of the two endpoints.

All other marked points are retained, and the three cuts preserve convexity.
Call the resulting body K'. With J(L)=integral_L(W-4/9), the removed heavy
parts have positive integrand, so

    J(K)>=J(K').                                         (2)

The three heavy chord halfplanes form a bounded triangle T, with

    H subset K' subset T,       T intersect (-T)=H.

For explicit boundedness in the coordinates above, their normals may be
taken as (b,1-a),(-1,1),(b-1,-a), with positive right sides b,1,a.
The positive coefficients 1+a-b, a+b-1, 1+b-a sum these normals to zero.
They span the plane, so the intersection is bounded, and zero is strictly
inside it. Its three reflected halfplanes are precisely the other three
hexagon edges, proving T intersect (-T)=H.

The three components Q_i of T outside H are disjoint triangular corners,
and they lie in the three light sectors. Boundary overlaps have area zero.
It remains to control the areas A_i=|K' intersect Q_i|, each between zero
and |Q_i|. No assertion that arbitrary triples of such areas are geometrically
realizable is needed; enlarging to the entire box gives a valid lower bound.

## 4. Exact barycentric formulas

Let v_0,v_1,v_2 be the vertices of T in counterclockwise order, and write
0=sum_i l_i v_i, with l_i>0 and sum l_i=1. The six sides of the strict
hexagon T intersect (-T) imply l_i<1/2. Equivalently put

    t_i=1-2l_i>0,       sum_i t_i=1,
    e=t_0 t_1+t_0 t_2+t_1 t_2>0.

In barycentric coordinates lambda_i of T, its reflection imposes
lambda_i<=2l_i=1-t_i. Thus its removed corner Q_i has relative area t_i^2,
and

    |Q_i|/|T|=t_i^2,       |H|/|T|=1-sum_i t_i^2=2e.      (3)

After the consistent cyclic labeling of the light caps, their chord vectors
are, for cyclic (i,j,k),

    p_i=t_k v_i+(1-t_k)v_k,
    -p_i=t_j v_i+(1-t_j)v_j.

These equalities describe the intersections of an edge of T with a reflected
edge. The cap R(p_i) dot x>=0 contains corner v_i and neither other corner.
For instance det(p_i,v_i)=(1-t_k)det(v_k,v_i)>0; the other two signs follow
from det(v_j,v_k)=2|T|l_i and are negative.

The unique positive normalized dependence among these three noncollinear
vectors has coefficients

    theta_i=t_i(1-t_i)/(2e).                              (4)

Their sum is one. To verify the balance directly, the coefficient of v_i
in sum theta_j p_j is

    [t_i(1-t_i)t_k+t_j(1-t_j)(1-t_i)]/(2e)
       =(1-t_i)/2=l_i.

Thus the vector sum is zero. This proves (4) without assuming any equal
chord lengths or equal weights.

Since H is centrally symmetric, W(x)+W(-x)=1 off the three cap lines,
so integral_H W=|H|/2. If a subset I of the light corners were filled
completely and the others omitted, its area ratio would therefore be

    F_I=[e+sum_(i in I) theta_i t_i^2]
          /[2e+sum_(i in I) t_i^2].                       (5)

For general A_i in their box, the same expression has t_i^2 replaced by
A_i/|T|. A linear-fractional function with strictly positive denominator
has a minimum at a box vertex: with the other variables fixed it is monotone
or constant in any one variable, so successively choose an endpoint. It
therefore suffices to prove F_I>=4/9 for all eight subsets I.

## 5. All eight subset inequalities

After multiplying F_I-4/9 by its positive denominator times 18e, the
required numerator is

    E_I=2e^2+sum_(i in I) t_i^2[9t_i(1-t_i)-8e].          (6)

For I empty this is positive. For all three indices, symmetric polynomial
identities give E_I=e-9t_0t_1t_2. It is nonnegative because
(sum t_i)(sum 1/t_i)>=9. Equality in this positive case requires all t_i=1/3.

For a singleton write its coordinate t, put s=1-t, v equal to the product
of the other two coordinates, and A=ts. Then 0<v<=s^2/4, e=A+v, and

    E=2(A+v)^2+t^2(A-8v)
      =2(v+A-2t^2)^2+t^3(9-17t).                         (7)

If t<=1/2 this is positive. If t>=1/2, its derivative with respect to v is
4(v+t-3t^2)<0 throughout 0<=v<=s^2/4, since 11t^2-2t-1>0 there.
The minimum over that interval is consequently at v=s^2/4, where

    E=s[1+5t-13t^2+15t^3]/8>0.

The bracketed cubic is positive for t>=0: its derivative
45t^2-26t+5 has negative discriminant and is positive, and the cubic
starts at one.

For two included indices let t be the omitted coordinate, s=1-t, and
v the product of the included coordinates. Expansion of (6) gives

    E=s[ts(1+t)+(1-8t)v].                                (8)

If t<=1/8 this is positive. Otherwise it is minimized at v=s^2/4 and

    E>=s^2(1-5t+12t^2)/4>0,

because the quadratic has negative discriminant and positive leading
coefficient. This proves all eight cases. Equations (2)--(6) prove (1)
for a strict noncollinear triple.

## 6. The half-weight degeneracy and general convex boundaries

The preceding chord cuts and area argument already permit nonsmooth K.
There is a direct treatment when, say, theta_3=1/2. Balance puts p_3 in
the relative interior of [-p_1,-p_2] and -p_3 in [p_1,p_2]. Because those
interior segment points are boundary points, the two parallel lines through
these segments support K. Now H=conv{±p_1,±p_2} is a parallelogram. Any part
of K outside H lies beyond its other pair of opposite edges, in their two
angular sectors, since the first edge pair already supports K. Both those
sectors have weighted indicator 1/2. Symmetry gives the same average on H.
Thus in this case the weighted cap average is exactly 1/2, which proves
the desired bound strictly.

Alternatively, the following limit preserves all individual centroidal
chords and proves the weak inequality without a separate strip argument.
Let p_K be the gauge of K about zero and define

    K_epsilon={x:(1-epsilon)p_K(x)+epsilon|x|<=1},
             0<epsilon<1.

Its gauge is strictly convex on noncollinear rays, so K_epsilon is strictly
convex. It converges to K in Hausdorff distance: the gauges converge uniformly
on the unit circle and are uniformly bounded above and below there.
For each original marked vector set

    c_i=1-epsilon+epsilon|p_i|,
    p_i^epsilon=p_i/c_i,
    theta_i^epsilon=theta_i c_i/(sum_j theta_j c_j).

Both ±p_i^epsilon lie on boundary K_epsilon, the weights sum to one, and
sum theta_i^epsilon p_i^epsilon=0. In a noncollinear triple all these weights
are strictly less than one half, by the strict-convexity version of the
argument in Section 2. Hence the already proved inequality applies.

The cap directions are unchanged, since the p_i were only multiplied by
positive scalars. Convex-body indicators converge in L1 and the weights
converge, so passing to the limit gives (1) exactly. This retains closed
halfspaces: their planar boundary lines have area zero.

For sharpness take T to be any triangle and place zero at its centroid.
Then t_i=1/3, theta_i=1/3, K=T, and (5) with all corners filled is exactly
4/9. Every displayed chord has zero as its midpoint, so all the theorem's
hypotheses are met.

For a noncollinear triple, equality can occur only in this triangle case.
The proper-subset inequalities are strict, so every light corner is filled,
the full-subset equality forces t_i=1/3, and no positive-area heavy piece
could have been removed in (2). Compact convexity then gives K=T. The
half-weight and opposite-pair cases have value 1/2 and cannot give equality.
